Mission 1

Why does 82/38^(2/3) come out as exactly 4?

Make a guess: Why does 82/38^(2/3) come out as exactly 4?

Algebra · indices and surds

The laws of indices

  • Multiply, add the powers: am×an=am+na^m × aⁿ = a^(m+n). Divide, subtract: am÷an=am−na^m ÷ aⁿ = a^(m−n).
  • Power of a power, multiply: (am)n=amn(a^m)ⁿ = a^mn.
  • Zero and negative indices: a0=1a⁰ = 1 and a−n=an1​a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, e.g. 2−3=81​2⁻³ = 1/8.
  • The laws need the same base: 23×322³ × 3² cannot be combined into one power.
Algebra · indices and surds

Fractional indices

  • (a1/n)n=an1​×n=a1(a^(1/n))ⁿ = a^(1/n × n) = a¹, so a1/na^(1/n) is the nnth root: an1​=na​a^(1/n) = n√a.
  • Then anm​=(na​)m=nam​a^(m/n) = (n√a)^m = n√(a^m). The denominator is the root, the numerator is the power.
  • Root first keeps numbers small: 272/3=(327​)2=32=927^(2/3) = (∛27)² = 3² = 9.
  • Index form is how A-level writes roots: x​=x21​√x = x^(1/2) and x​1​=x−21​1/(√x) = x^(−1/2).
Worked example Algebra · indices and surds

A negative fractional index

Question
Without a calculator, evaluate (8116​)−43​(16/81)^(−3/4).
  1. 1
    Deal with the minus sign by taking the reciprocal: (1681​)43​(81/16)^(3/4)
  2. 2
    Take the fourth root of top and bottom: 416​481​​=23​(∜81)/(∜16) = 3/2
  3. 3
    Cube: (23​)3=827​(3/2)³ = 27/8
Answer
827​27/8
⚠️ Watch out
a negative index means "reciprocal", not "negative number". (8116​)−3/4(16/81)^(−3/4) is positive.

Algebra · indices and surds

Simplifying surds

  • A surd is an irrational root such as 2​√2. Keep it exact.
  • ab​=a​b​√ab = √a√b and ba​​=b​a​​√(a/b) = (√a)/(√b). Take out the largest square factor: 72​=36​2​=62​√72 = √36√2 = 6√2.
  • (a​)2=a(√a)² = a and (x​+y​)(x​−y​)=x−y(√x + √y)(√x − √y) = x − y.
  • Never split a sum: a+b​=a​+b​√(a + b) ≠ √a + √b.
Worked example Algebra · indices and surds

Rationalising the denominator

Question
Express 3−2​5​5/(3 − √2) in the form ca+b2​​(a + b√2)/c, where aa, bb and cc are integers.
  1. 1
    Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate 3+2​3 + √2: (3−2​)(3+2​)5(3+2​)​(5(3 + √2))/((3 − √2)(3 + √2))
  2. 2
    Difference of two squares on the bottom: 9−2=79 − 2 = 7
  3. 3
    Expand the top: 15+52​15 + 5√2
Answer
715+52​​(15 + 5√2)/7
⚠️ Watch out
multiplying by 3−2​3 − √2 gives (3−2​)2=11−62​(3 − √2)² = 11 − 6√2 on the bottom, which is still irrational. Change the sign.
Calculate

Mission check

?Why does 82/38^(2/3) come out as exactly 4?

Three copies of 81/38^(1/3) multiply to 81=88¹ = 8, so 81/38^(1/3) is the cube root of 8, which is 2. Then 82/3=(81/3)2=22=48^(2/3) = (8^(1/3))² = 2² = 4. The denominator of a fractional index is a root and the numerator is a power.

Mission 2

A ball's height is h=20t−5t2h = 20t − 5t². Does it ever reach 25 m?

Make a guess: A ball's height is h=20t−5t2h = 20t − 5t². Does it ever reach 25 m?

Algebra · quadratics and the discriminant

Completing the square

  • Write ax2+bx+cax² + bx + c as a(x+p)2+qa(x + p)² + q. For a=1a = 1: halve the xx-coefficient, then correct the constant: x2+6x+2=(x+3)2−9+2=(x+3)2−7x² + 6x + 2 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 2 = (x + 3)² − 7.
  • If a=1a ≠ 1, take aa out of the x2x² and xx terms first.
  • The turning point of y=a(x+p)2+qy = a(x + p)² + q is (−p,q)(−p, q), on the line of symmetry x=−px = −p.
  • a>0a > 0: a minimum, value qq. a<0a < 0: a maximum, value qq.
Worked example Algebra · quadratics and the discriminant

Turning point from the completed square

Question
Write 2x2−12x+232x² − 12x + 23 in the form a(x+p)2+qa(x + p)² + q. Hence state the turning point of y=2x2−12x+23y = 2x² − 12x + 23 and explain why the equation 2x2−12x+23=02x² − 12x + 23 = 0 has no real roots.
  1. 1
    Take out the 2 from the first two terms: 2(x2−6x)+232(x² − 6x) + 23
  2. 2
    Complete the square inside: 2[(x−3)2−9]+232[(x − 3)² − 9] + 23
  3. 3
    Expand the bracket's constant: 2(x−3)2−18+23=2(x−3)2+52(x − 3)² − 18 + 23 = 2(x − 3)² + 5
  4. 4
    Read off: minimum point (3,5)(3, 5). Since 2(x−3)2≥02(x − 3)² ≥ 0, y≥5>0y ≥ 5 > 0 for every xx.
Answer
2(x−3)2+52(x − 3)² + 5; turning point (3,5)(3, 5), a minimum; the curve never reaches y=0y = 0, so there are no real roots.
⚠️ Watch out
the −9−9 inside the square bracket must be multiplied by 2. Writing 2(x−3)2−9+232(x − 3)² − 9 + 23 gives the wrong qq.
Calculate
?By completing the square, find the maximum value of y=3+8x−2x2y = 3 + 8x − 2x².
Algebra · quadratics and the discriminant

The discriminant

  • For ax2+bx+c=0ax² + bx + c = 0 the discriminant is b2−4acb² − 4ac, the part under the root in x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a.
  • b2−4ac>0b² − 4ac > 0: two distinct real roots; the graph crosses the xx-axis twice.
  • b2−4ac=0b² − 4ac = 0: one repeated root; the graph touches the xx-axis.
  • b2−4ac<0b² − 4ac < 0: no real roots; the graph misses the xx-axis.
  • "Real roots" means b2−4ac≥0b² − 4ac ≥ 0.
Quick check
?Find the discriminant of 3x2+5x+43x² + 5x + 4. What does it tell you about 3x2+5x+4=03x² + 5x + 4 = 0?
Worked example Algebra · quadratics and the discriminant

Finding kk for equal roots

Question
The equation x2+kx+k+3=0x² + kx + k + 3 = 0 has equal roots. Find the possible values of kk.
  1. 1
    Identify the coefficients: a=1a = 1, b=kb = k, c=k+3c = k + 3
  2. 2
    Equal roots, so set the discriminant to zero: k2−4(k+3)=0k² − 4(k + 3) = 0
  3. 3
    Simplify and factorise: k2−4k−12=0k² − 4k − 12 = 0, so (k−6)(k+2)=0(k − 6)(k + 2) = 0
  4. 4
    Check: k=6k = 6 gives (x+3)2=0(x + 3)² = 0; k=−2k = −2 gives (x−1)2=0(x − 1)² = 0.
Answer
k=6k = 6 or k=−2k = −2
⚠️ Watch out
cc is the whole constant term k+3k + 3, not just 3. Using c=3c = 3 gives k2−12=0k² − 12 = 0.
Calculate
?The equation kx2+6x+k=0kx² + 6x + k = 0, where kk is a positive constant, has a repeated root. Find kk.
Algebra · quadratics and the discriminant

Quadratics in disguise

  • An equation is a quadratic in a function of xx if it fits a(…)2+b(…)+c=0a(…)² + b(…) + c = 0.
  • x4−5x2+4=0x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0: let u=x2u = x², so u2−5u+4=0u² − 5u + 4 = 0, u=1u = 1 or 44, and x=±1x = ± 1 or ±2± 2.
  • x−5x​+6=0x − 5√x + 6 = 0: let u=x​u = √x, since x=(x​)2x = (√x)².
  • Solve for uu, then convert back to xx. Reject impossible values: x2x² and x​√x cannot be negative.
  • Later you will meet the same idea with sinxsin x, exe^x and lnxln x.
Calculate
?Solve x−2x​−8=0x − 2√x − 8 = 0.
Mission check

?A ball's height is h=20t−5t2h = 20t − 5t². Does it ever reach 25 m?

Completing the square gives h=20−5(t−2)2h = 20 − 5(t − 2)², so the ball peaks at 20 m when t=2t = 2 and never reaches 25 m. The discriminant agrees: h=25h = 25 gives 5t2−20t+25=05t² − 20t + 25 = 0, with b2−4ac=−100<0b² − 4ac = −100 < 0, so there is no time when h=25h = 25.

Mission 3

When does a line just touch a curve, and what one number tells you?

Make a guess: When does a line just touch a curve, and what one number tells you?

Algebra · simultaneous equations and inequalities

One linear, one quadratic

  • Two linear equations: eliminate a variable by adding or subtracting multiples, or substitute.
  • One linear, one quadratic: use substitution. Make xx or yy the subject of the linear equation; substitute into the quadratic.
  • Solve the quadratic, then put each value into the linear equation for its partner. Give answers in pairs: each is a meeting point.
  • The substituted quadratic's discriminant counts the meeting points: >0> 0 two, =0= 0 one (the line is a tangent), <0< 0 none.
Worked example Algebra · simultaneous equations and inequalities

Where a line meets a parabola

Question
Solve the simultaneous equations y=2x+3y = 2x + 3 and y=x2−4x+8y = x² − 4x + 8.
  1. 1
    Substitute for yy: 2x+3=x2−4x+82x + 3 = x² − 4x + 8
  2. 2
    Rearrange to zero: x2−6x+5=0x² − 6x + 5 = 0
  3. 3
    Factorise: (x−1)(x−5)=0(x − 1)(x − 5) = 0, so x=1x = 1 or x=5x = 5
  4. 4
    Find each yy from the linear equation: x=1x = 1 gives y=5y = 5; x=5x = 5 gives y=13y = 13
Answer
x=1,y=5x = 1, y = 5 and x=5,y=13x = 5, y = 13
⚠️ Watch out
listing x=1x = 1, x=5x = 5, y=5y = 5, y=13y = 13 without pairing them loses the final mark.
Calculate
?The line y=4x+cy = 4x + c is a tangent to the curve y=x2+2x+5y = x² + 2x + 5. Find the value of the constant cc.
Algebra · simultaneous equations and inequalities

Solving inequalities

  • Linear: solve like an equation, but reverse the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number.
  • Quadratic: find the critical values (solve =0= 0), sketch the parabola, then read off where it is above (>0> 0) or below (<0< 0) the xx-axis.
  • px2+qx+r<ax+bpx² + qx + r < ax + b means the curve is below the line: rearrange to one side first.
  • With xx in a denominator, multiply by x2x² (positive, since x=0x ≠ 0), not xx (its sign is unknown): x6​<26/x < 2 gives 6x<2x26x < 2x², so x<0x < 0 or x>3x > 3.
Worked example Algebra · simultaneous equations and inequalities

A quadratic inequality

Question
Solve x2−2x−15>0x² − 2x − 15 > 0. Give your answer in set notation.
  1. 1
    Find the critical values: (x+3)(x−5)=0(x + 3)(x − 5) = 0, so x=−3x = −3 or x=5x = 5
  2. 2
    Sketch: a ∪∪-shaped parabola crossing the xx-axis at −3−3 and 55.
  3. 3
    Read off where the curve is above the axis: to the left of −3−3 and to the right of 5.
  4. 4
    Write it as two separate parts joined by "or": x<−3x < −3 or x>5x > 5
Answer
{x:x<−3}∪{x:x>5}{x : x < −3} ∪ {x : x > 5}
⚠️ Watch out
writing −3>x>5−3 > x > 5 is wrong: no number is less than −3−3 and greater than 5 at once.
Algebra · simultaneous equations and inequalities

Set notation and interval notation

  • {x:x>3}{x : x > 3} means "the set of xx such that x>3x > 3".
  • "or" joins two parts with ∪∪: {x:x<−3}∪{x:x>5}{x : x < −3} ∪ {x : x > 5}.
  • "and" overlaps two conditions, ∩∩: {x:x>−3}∩{x:x≤2}={x:−3<x≤2}{x : x > −3} ∩ {x : x ≤ 2} = {x : −3 < x ≤ 2}.
  • ∅∅ is the empty set: no values work.
  • Interval notation: (a,b)(a, b) means a<x<ba < x < b; [a,b][a, b] means a≤x≤ba ≤ x ≤ b; [a,b)[a, b) means a≤x<ba ≤ x < b.
Quick check
?Which is the solution of x2+4x−21≤0x² + 4x − 21 ≤ 0?
Calculate
?How many integers xx satisfy both 3x−1>53x − 1 > 5 and x2−5x−14<0x² − 5x − 14 < 0?
Algebra · simultaneous equations and inequalities

Regions on a graph

  • To show y>x−1y > x − 1, draw the boundary y=x−1y = x − 1 and identify the side where the inequality holds.
  • A strict inequality (<<, >>) has a dashed boundary; ≤≤ or ≥≥ has a solid boundary.
  • Test a point not on the boundary, such as (0,0)(0, 0): 0>0−10 > 0 − 1 is true, so (0,0)(0, 0) is in the region.
  • Shade as the question instructs, and label the required region RR. Region RR in the diagram: y>x−1y > x − 1 and y≤5−x2y ≤ 5 − x².
Mission check

?When does a line just touch a curve, and what one number tells you?

Substitute the line into the curve to get one quadratic equation. Its roots are the meeting points, so the discriminant b2−4acb² − 4ac counts them: positive for two, zero for exactly one (the line just touches, as a tangent), negative for none.

Mission 4

x3−6x2+11x−6=0x³−6x²+11x−6=0 has an easy root. How do the other two follow?

Make a guess: x3−6x2+11x−6=0x³−6x²+11x−6=0 has an easy root. How do the other two follow?

Algebra · polynomials

The factor theorem

  • Factor theorem: f(a)=0⇔(x−a)f(a)=0 Leftrightarrow (x−a) is a factor of f(x)f(x).
  • More generally, f(ab​)=0⇔(ax−b)f(b/a)=0 Leftrightarrow (ax−b) is a factor.
  • A root of f(x)=0f(x)=0 is an xx-intercept of y=f(x)y=f(x).
  • To find a first root of a cubic, try the factors of the constant term: ±1,±2,±3,…±1, ±2, ±3, … If none work, try fractions ab​b/a, with bb a factor of the constant term and aa a factor of the leading coefficient.
Worked example Algebra · polynomials

Show that, hence factorise

Question
f(x)=x3+3x2−4f(x)=x³+3x²−4. Show that (x−1)(x−1) is a factor of f(x)f(x) and hence factorise f(x)f(x) completely.
  1. 1
    Substitute x=1x=1: f(1)=1+3−4=0f(1)=1+3−4=0, so (x−1)(x−1) is a factor by the factor theorem.
  2. 2
    Divide by (x−1)(x−1), writing the missing xx term as 0x0x: x3+3x2+0x−4=(x−1)(x2+4x+4)x³+3x²+0x−4 = (x−1)(x²+4x+4)
  3. 3
    Factorise the quadratic: x2+4x+4=(x+2)2x²+4x+4=(x+2)²
Answer
f(x)=(x−1)(x+2)2f(x)=(x−1)(x+2)², so the graph crosses the xx-axis at 1 and touches it at −2−2.
⚠️ Watch out
forgetting the 0x0x placeholder makes the columns of the division slip.
Algebra · polynomials

Algebraic division by a linear factor

  • Divide f(x)f(x) by (x−a)(x−a) with long division, or compare coefficients in f(x)≡(x−a)(px2+qx+r)f(x) ≡ (x−a)(px²+qx+r).
  • Match x3x³ terms for pp, constants for rr, then x2x² terms for qq.
  • Dividing a cubic by a linear factor leaves a quadratic quotient.
  • A-level only: to simplify a rational expression, factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel common factors, never single terms.
Quick check

Calculate

A cubic with a fractional root

Question
Solve 6x3+11x2−x−6=06x³+11x²−x−6=0.
  1. 1
    Try factors of −6−6: f(1)=10f(1)=10, but f(−1)=−6+11+1−6=0f(−1)=−6+11+1−6=0, so (x+1)(x+1) is a factor.
  2. 2
    Divide: 6x3+11x2−x−6=(x+1)(6x2+5x−6)6x³+11x²−x−6=(x+1)(6x²+5x−6)
  3. 3
    Factorise the quadratic: 6x2+5x−6=(2x+3)(3x−2)6x²+5x−6=(2x+3)(3x−2)
  4. 4
    Set each factor to zero: x=−1x=−1, x=−23​x=−3/2, x=32​x=2/3
Answer
x=−1x=−1, x=−23​x=−3/2 or x=32​x=2/3 (check: f(32​)=0f(2/3)=0, so (3x−2)(3x−2) is a factor).
⚠️ Watch out
a cubic can have roots that are fractions; trying only whole numbers can miss them.
Calculate

Mission check

?x3−6x2+11x−6=0x³−6x²+11x−6=0 has the easy root x=1x=1. How do the other two roots follow?

Since f(1)=0f(1)=0, the factor theorem says (x−1)(x−1) is a factor. Dividing it out leaves the quadratic x2−5x+6=(x−2)(x−3)x²−5x+6=(x−2)(x−3), so the other roots are 2 and 3.

Mission 5

y=f(2x)y=f(2x) is narrower, but y=2f(x)y=2f(x) is taller. Why opposite?

Make a guess: y=f(2x)y=f(2x) is narrower, but y=2f(x)y=2f(x) is taller. Why opposite?

Algebra · graphs and transformations

Sketching cubics and quartics

  • From factorised form, each factor gives an xx-intercept; put x=0x=0 for the yy-intercept.
  • A single factor: the curve crosses the axis. A repeated root (squared factor): the curve touches the axis and turns.
  • The sign of the leading term fixes the ends: a positive cubic rises from bottom left to top right; a positive quartic goes up at both ends.
Quick check
?Which statement describes the graph of y=(x+3)(x−1)2y=(x+3)(x−1)²?
Algebra · graphs and transformations

Reciprocal graphs, asymptotes and intersections

  • y=xa​y=a/x (with a>0a>0): two branches, in the first and third quadrants.
  • y=x2a​y=a/x² (with a>0a>0): both branches above the xx-axis.
  • Both have asymptotes x=0x=0 and y=0y=0: lines the curve approaches but never meets.
  • The solutions of f(x)=g(x)f(x)=g(x) are the xx-coordinates of the intersection points of y=f(x)y=f(x) and y=g(x)y=g(x); count intersections to count solutions.
  • Proportion: y∝xy ∝ x means y=kxy=kx (a line through the origin); y∝x1​y ∝ 1/x means y=xk​y=k/x; y∝x21​y ∝ 1/x² means y=x2k​y=k/x².
Algebra · graphs and transformations

Transformations of y=f(x)y=f(x)

EquationTransformationPoint (x,y)(x, y) goes to
y=f(x)+ay=f(x)+atranslation (0a​)(0; a)(x, y+a)(x, y+a)
y=f(x+a)y=f(x+a)translation (−a0​)(−a; 0)(x−a, y)(x−a, y)
y=af(x)y=af(x)stretch parallel to the yy-axis, scale factor aa(x, ay)(x, ay)
y=f(ax)y=f(ax)stretch parallel to the xx-axis, scale factor a1​1/a(ax​, y)(x/a, y)
  • Changes outside the bracket act on yy as you expect. Changes inside act on xx and work in reverse.
  • y=−f(x)y=−f(x) reflects in the xx-axis; y=f(−x)y=f(−x) reflects in the yy-axis.

Where does the maximum go?

Question
The curve y=f(x)y=f(x) has a maximum point at (4,6)(4, 6). Find the maximum point on each of y=f(2x)y=f(2x), y=2f(x)y=2f(x), y=f(x+3)y=f(x+3) and y=f(x)−5y=f(x)−5.
  1. 1
    y=f(2x)y=f(2x): stretch parallel to the xx-axis, scale factor 21​1/2, so halve xx: (2,6)(2, 6)
  2. 2
    y=2f(x)y=2f(x): stretch parallel to the yy-axis, scale factor 2, so double yy: (4,12)(4, 12)
  3. 3
    y=f(x+3)y=f(x+3): translation (−30​)(−3; 0): (1,6)(1, 6)
  4. 4
    y=f(x)−5y=f(x)−5: translation (0−5​)(0; −5): (4,1)(4, 1)
Answer
(2,6)(2, 6), (4,12)(4, 12), (1,6)(1, 6) and (4,1)(4, 1)

Combining transformations (A-level only)

Question
The point P(2,5)P(2, 5) lies on y=f(x)y=f(x). Find the image of PP on the curve y=3f(x+1)−4y=3f(x+1)−4.
  1. 1
    Inside the bracket: x+1x+1 translates by (−10​)(−1; 0): (1,5)(1, 5)
  2. 2
    Multiply the output by 3 (stretch parallel to the yy-axis): (1,15)(1, 15)
  3. 3
    Subtract 4 (translation (0−4​)(0; −4)): (1,11)(1, 11)
Answer
(1,11)(1, 11)
⚠️ Watch out
the yy-coordinate is 3×5−4=113 × 5 − 4 = 11. Subtracting first, 3(5−4)=33(5−4)=3, is the transformation y=3(f(x+1)−4)y=3(f(x+1)−4), a different curve.
Sort it
?Does each graph come from changing the xx-coordinates or the yy-coordinates of y=f(x)y=f(x)?

Tap a statement, then tap the group it belongs in. Then press Check.

Mission check

?Why does the 2 make y=f(2x)y=f(2x) narrower but y=2f(x)y=2f(x) taller?

In y=f(2x)y=f(2x) the input is doubled, so each output is reached when xx is half as big: the graph is squashed by scale factor 21​1/2 towards the yy-axis. In y=2f(x)y=2f(x) the output is doubled after the function, so the graph is stretched by scale factor 2 away from the xx-axis.

Algebra · functions

Functions, domain and range (A-level only)

  • A function maps every input in its domain to exactly one output. The set of all outputs is the range.
  • One-one: each output comes from only one input. Many-one: some output comes from two or more inputs, e.g. f(x)=x2f(x)=x², x∈Rx ∈ ℝ, has f(3)=f(−3)=9f(3)=f(−3)=9.
  • Notation: f:x↦x2f: x mapsto x² or f(x)=x2f(x)=x². Range: f(x)≥0f(x) ≥ 0.
  • To find a range, sketch the graph; for a quadratic, complete the square.
  • Modelling: the context sets a model's domain (e.g. time t≥0t ≥ 0). Unrealistic outputs show a limitation: refine the model.
Quick check
?f(x)=x2−6x+11f(x)=x²−6x+11, x∈Rx ∈ ℝ. What is the range of ff?
Algebra · functions

Composite and inverse functions

  • fg(x)=f(g(x))fg(x)=f(g(x)): do gg first, then ff. Usually fg(x)=gf(x)fg(x) ≠ gf(x).
  • The inverse f−1f⁻¹ undoes ff: f−1f(x)=xf⁻¹f(x)=x. Only one-one functions have an inverse.
  • To find f−1(x)f⁻¹(x): write y=f(x)y=f(x), rearrange to make xx the subject, then swap xx and yy.
  • Domain of f−1f⁻¹ = range of ff; range of f−1f⁻¹ = domain of ff.
  • The graph of y=f−1(x)y=f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y=f(x)y=f(x) in the line y=xy=x.
Worked example Algebra · functions

An inverse with a restricted domain

Question
f(x)=(x−2)2+1f(x)=(x−2)²+1, x≥2x ≥ 2. Find f−1(x)f⁻¹(x) and state its domain.
  1. 1
    Range of ff: the least value is f(2)=1f(2)=1, so f(x)≥1f(x) ≥ 1.
  2. 2
    Write y=(x−2)2+1y=(x−2)²+1 and rearrange: (x−2)2=y−1(x−2)²=y−1
  3. 3
    Since x≥2x ≥ 2, take the positive root: x=2+y−1​x=2+√(y−1)
  4. 4
    Swap xx and yy: f−1(x)=2+x−1​f⁻¹(x)=2+√(x−1)
Answer
f−1(x)=2+x−1​f⁻¹(x)=2+√(x−1), with domain x≥1x ≥ 1 (the range of ff).
⚠️ Watch out
keeping ±± gives two outputs; the domain x≥2x ≥ 2 tells you to use the ++ root.
Calculate

Algebra · functions

The modulus function

  • ∣x∣|x| is the size of xx without its sign: ∣−4∣=4|−4|=4.
  • Sketch y=∣ax+b∣y=|ax+b|: draw y=ax+by=ax+b, then reflect the part below the xx-axis in the xx-axis. You get a V with vertex (−ab​,0)(−b/a, 0).
  • Solve ∣f(x)∣=g(x)|f(x)|=g(x): solve f(x)=g(x)f(x)=g(x) and −f(x)=g(x)−f(x)=g(x), then check each answer in the original. A sketch shows how many solutions to expect.
Worked example Algebra · functions

A modulus equation with a false root

Question
Solve ∣x−3∣=2x+1|x−3|=2x+1.
  1. 1
    Case x−3=2x+1x−3=2x+1: x=−4x=−4. Check: 2(−4)+1=−72(−4)+1=−7, but a modulus is never negative, so reject it.
  2. 2
    Case −(x−3)=2x+1−(x−3)=2x+1: 3−x=2x+13−x=2x+1, so x=32​x=2/3.
  3. 3
    Check: ​32​−3​=37​|2/3−3|=7/3 and 2(32​)+1=37​2(2/3)+1=7/3. It works.
Answer
x=32​x=2/3 only; the graphs meet once.
⚠️ Watch out
solving both cases is not enough. Always check, because one case can give a false root.
Calculate
?Solve ∣2x−7∣=x+1|2x−7|=x+1. Give the smaller solution.
Mission check

?Why must y=x2y=x² lose half its domain before it has an inverse?

On all of Rℝ, x2x² is many-one: 33 and −3−3 both map to 9, so an "inverse" would have to send 9 to two places, which no function can do. Restricting the domain to x≥0x ≥ 0 makes x2x² one-one, and its inverse is x​√x, the reflection in y=xy=x.

Algebra · partial fractions

Splitting a fraction (A-level only)

  • Adding fractions makes one denominator: n1​−n+11​=n(n+1)1​1/n−1/(n+1)=1/(n(n+1)). Partial fractions reverse this.
  • Distinct linear factors: (ax+b)(cx+d)px+q​≡ax+bA​+cx+dB​(px+q)/((ax+b)(cx+d)) ≡ A/(ax+b)+B/(cx+d), and similarly with three factors.
  • Multiply through by the denominator to get an identity, then substitute the value of xx that makes each factor zero (or compare coefficients).
  • Here the numerator is constant or linear: lower degree than the denominator.
Worked example Algebra · partial fractions

Two linear factors

Question
Express (x−1)(x+2)5x+1​(5x+1)/((x−1)(x+2)) in partial fractions.
  1. 1
    Write the form: (x−1)(x+2)5x+1​≡x−1A​+x+2B​(5x+1)/((x−1)(x+2)) ≡ A/(x−1)+B/(x+2)
  2. 2
    Multiply by (x−1)(x+2)(x−1)(x+2): 5x+1≡A(x+2)+B(x−1)5x+1 ≡ A(x+2)+B(x−1)
  3. 3
    Put x=1x=1: 6=3A6=3A, so A=2A=2
  4. 4
    Put x=−2x=−2: −9=−3B−9=−3B, so B=3B=3
Answer
x−12​+x+23​2/(x−1)+3/(x+2)
⚠️ Watch out
the identity holds for every xx, so you may substitute x=1x=1 even though the original fraction is undefined there.
Calculate
?(2x+1)(x−3)7x−7​≡2x+1A​+x−3B​(7x−7)/((2x+1)(x−3)) ≡ A/(2x+1)+B/(x−3). Find the value of AA.
Algebra · partial fractions

Repeated linear factors

  • A squared factor needs two fractions: (ax+b)(cx+d)2px+q​≡ax+bA​+cx+dB​+(cx+d)2C​(px+q)/((ax+b)(cx+d)²) ≡ A/(ax+b)+B/(cx+d)+C/((cx+d)²)
  • Multiply through by the whole denominator; the BB term keeps one factor of (cx+d)(cx+d).
  • Substituting the two roots gives AA and CC. Find BB by comparing coefficients of x2x², or by substituting another value such as x=0x=0.
Worked example Algebra · partial fractions

A repeated factor

Question
Express (x+1)(x−1)24​4/((x+1)(x−1)²) in partial fractions.
  1. 1
    Form: (x+1)(x−1)24​≡x+1A​+x−1B​+(x−1)2C​4/((x+1)(x−1)²) ≡ A/(x+1)+B/(x−1)+C/((x−1)²)
  2. 2
    Multiply through: 4≡A(x−1)2+B(x+1)(x−1)+C(x+1)4 ≡ A(x−1)²+B(x+1)(x−1)+C(x+1)
  3. 3
    Put x=1x=1: 4=2C4=2C, so C=2C=2. Put x=−1x=−1: 4=4A4=4A, so A=1A=1.
  4. 4
    Compare x2x² coefficients: 0=A+B0=A+B, so B=−1B=−1
Answer
x+11​−x−11​+(x−1)22​1/(x+1)−1/(x−1)+2/((x−1)²)
⚠️ Watch out
there is no x2x² term on the left, so its coefficient is 0, not 4.
Quick check
?Which form is correct for splitting x(x+2)23x+2​(3x+2)/(x(x+2)²) into partial fractions?
Calculate

Give your answer as a decimal.

Algebra · partial fractions

Why split fractions?

  • Integration: each simple fraction integrates to a logarithm, e.g. x−12​+x+23​2/(x−1)+3/(x+2).
  • Series: expand each simple fraction with the binomial expansion, then add.
  • Sums that cancel: n(n+1)1​=n1​−n+11​1/(n(n+1))=1/n−1/(n+1). Write each term of a sum this way and neighbouring pieces cancel, leaving only the first and last.
Calculate
?Use n(n+1)1​=n1​−n+11​1/(n(n+1))=1/n−1/(n+1) to find 2×31​+3×41​+⋯+9×101​1/(2×3)+1/(3×4)+…+1/(9×10).

Give your answer as a decimal.

Mission check

?Why is 1×21​+2×31​+⋯+99×1001​1/(1×2)+1/(2×3)+…+1/(99×100) so neat?

Partial fractions give n(n+1)1​=n1​−n+11​1/(n(n+1))=1/n−1/(n+1). Written this way, each −n+11​−1/(n+1) cancels the next term's +n+11​+1/(n+1), so only 1−1001​=10099​1−1/100=99/100 survives.

Recap

Big ideas

  • am×an=am+na^m × aⁿ = a^(m+n), am÷an=am−na^m ÷ aⁿ = a^(m−n), (am)n=amn(a^m)ⁿ = a^mn, a0=1a⁰ = 1, a−n=an1​a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
  • anm​=(na​)ma^(m/n) = (n√a)^m: denominator root, numerator power; negative index means reciprocal.
  • Simplify surds with ab​=a​b​√ab = √a√b; rationalise p−q​1​1/(p − √q) by multiplying by p+q​p + √q.
  • Completing the square, a(x+p)2+qa(x + p)² + q, gives the turning point (−p,q)(−p, q) and the greatest or least value.
  • The discriminant b2−4acb² − 4ac decides the roots: >0> 0 two distinct, =0= 0 repeated, <0< 0 none.
  • Spot quadratics in x2x² or x​√x, substitute uu, and reject impossible values.
  • Linear and quadratic together: substitute, solve the quadratic, pair each xx with its yy; the discriminant counts the meeting points.
  • Quadratic inequalities: find the critical values, sketch, read off; "or" is ∪∪, "and" is ∩∩.
  • Regions: dashed boundary for << or >>, solid for ≤≤ or ≥≥; test a point to pick the side.
  • Factor theorem: f(a)=0⇔(x−a)f(a)=0 Leftrightarrow (x−a) is a factor, and f(ab​)=0⇔(ax−b)f(b/a)=0 Leftrightarrow (ax−b) is a factor.
  • Find one root by trial, divide (or compare coefficients) to get a quadratic, then factorise or solve it.
  • Factorised polynomials: single roots cross, repeated roots touch; y=xa​y=a/x and y=x2a​y=a/x² have asymptotes x=0x=0 and y=0y=0.
  • Outside the bracket acts on yy as written; inside acts on xx in reverse: f(x+a)f(x+a) moves left, f(ax)f(ax) has scale factor a1​1/a.
  • Intersections of two graphs give the solutions of f(x)=g(x)f(x)=g(x).
  • A function gives one output per input; only one-one functions have inverses, so a many-one function needs its domain restricted first.
  • fg(x)fg(x) means do gg first; y=f−1(x)y=f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y=f(x)y=f(x) in y=xy=x, and their domain and range swap.
  • For ∣f(x)∣=g(x)|f(x)|=g(x), solve both cases and check each answer.
  • Distinct linear factors give one fraction each; a squared factor (cx+d)2(cx+d)² needs both cx+dB​B/(cx+d) and (cx+d)2C​C/((cx+d)²).
  • Multiply through to an identity, substitute the roots, then compare coefficients for any constant left.
  • Partial fractions make integrals, binomial expansions and some sums easy.
